sources.title: Nightmares
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Amy W. Anzilotti, MD, June 2023)
sources.quote: When kids wake up from a nightmare, its images are still fresh and can seem real. So it's natural for them to feel afraid and upset and to call out to a parent for comfort. ... a little comfort from you can quickly ease your child's mind and help them get back to sleep. ... Reassure your child that you're there. Your calm presence helps your child feel safe and protected after waking up feeling afraid. ... You might say something like, "You had a bad dream, but now you're awake and everything is OK." ... Show that you understand that your child feels afraid and it's OK. Remind your child that everyone dreams and sometimes the dreams are scary, upsetting, and can seem very real, so it's natural to feel scared by them. ... No need to talk more than briefly about the nightmare in the wee hours ... But in the morning, your child may want to tell you all about last night's scary dream. ... This might include a bath, a snuggle from you, reading, or some quiet talk about the pleasant events of the day. ... Talking about it — maybe even drawing the dream or writing about it — in the daylight can help scary images lose their power. Your child might enjoy thinking up a new (more satisfying) ending to the scary dream.
sources.supports: After a nightmare the images feel real and children call a parent; comfort eases them quickly; reassure that you are there; label it as a bad dream that is over; show it is OK to be afraid and that everyone dreams; talk only briefly at night and more in the morning; reading is part of a calming bedtime routine, and writing about the dream or a new ending helps in the daylight.

sources.title: Nightmares, Night Terrors & Sleepwalking in Children: How Parents Can Help
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 21 Sep 2023)
sources.quote: Children may wake up crying or feeling afraid and may have trouble falling back to sleep. If your child has a bad dream, the best response is to comfort them. ... Go to your child as quickly as you can. Assure them that you are there and will not let anything harm them. Encourage them to tell you what happened in the dream. Remind them that dreams are not real. ... Once your child is ready, encourage them to go back to sleep.
sources.supports: Comfort is the best response; go quickly; assure the child you are there and will not let anything harm them; let them tell what happened; remind them dreams are not real; encourage sleep once the child is ready.

sources.title: Nightmares
sources.publisher: AASM Sleep Education, American Academy of Sleep Medicine (October 2020, reviewed by Reeba Mathew, MD and Anne M. Morse, DO)
sources.quote: Nightmares are especially typical in children aged 3-6 years. Up to 50% of young children have severe nightmares that cause them to wake up their parents. ... Respond quickly to comfort your child when he or she wakes up from a nightmare. ... Assure your child that it is normal for children and even adults to have nightmares.
sources.supports: Nightmares are especially typical at ages 3 to 6; respond quickly; tell the child that children and adults have nightmares.

sources.title: Nightmares
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Amy W. Anzilotti, MD, June 2023)
sources.quote: When kids wake up from a nightmare, its images are still fresh and can seem real. So it's natural for them to feel afraid and upset and to call out to a parent for comfort. ... have a bed that's a cozy, peaceful place to quiet down. A favorite toy, stuffed animal, nightlight, or dream catcher can help. ... Go ahead and check the closet and under the bed, reassuring your child that all's clear. ... A nightlight or a hall light can help kids feel safe in a dark room as they get ready to go back to sleep. A bedside flashlight can be a good nightmare-chaser. ... offer a favorite stuffed animal to hold, a blanket, pillow, nightlight, or dreamcatcher, or play soft music. ... And maybe seal it by giving your child a kiss to hold — in the palm of their hand — as you tiptoe out of the room. ... This might include a bath, a snuggle from you, reading, or some quiet talk about the pleasant events of the day.
sources.supports: After a nightmare the images feel real; a cozy bed with a favorite toy or nightlight helps; check the closet and under the bed with the child; a nightlight, hall light or bedside flashlight helps the child feel safe going back to sleep; a stuffed animal or soft music; a kiss to hold in the palm while tiptoeing out; reading is part of a calming bedtime routine.

Go to your child as quickly as you can. ... Allow them to keep a light on if it makes them feel better. ... See if there is something that is scaring your child, like shadows. If so, make sure they are gone.

sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Amy W. Anzilotti, MD, June 2023)
sources.quote: A child might not remember every detail, but can usually recall some of the images, characters, or situations, and the scary parts. ... This might include a bath, a snuggle from you, reading, or some quiet talk about the pleasant events of the day. ... You also might talk about some pleasant dreams your child would like to have. ... No need to talk more than briefly about the nightmare in the wee hours — just help your child feel calm, safe, and protected, and ready to go back to sleep. But in the morning, your child may want to tell you all about last night's scary dream. Talking about it — maybe even drawing the dream or writing about it — in the daylight can help scary images lose their power. Your child might enjoy thinking up a new (more satisfying) ending to the scary dream. ... Remind your child that everyone dreams and sometimes the dreams are scary, upsetting, and can seem very real, so it's natural to feel scared by them.

sources.title: Nightmares
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Amy W. Anzilotti, MD, June 2023)
sources.quote: When kids wake up from a nightmare, its images are still fresh and can seem real. So it's natural for them to feel afraid and upset and to call out to a parent for comfort. By about preschool age, kids begin to understand that a nightmare is only a dream — and that what's happening isn't real and can't hurt them. But knowing that doesn't prevent them from feeling scared. ... You might say something like, "You had a bad dream, but now you're awake and everything is OK." ... Offer comfort. Show that you understand that your child feels afraid and it's OK. Remind your child that everyone dreams and sometimes the dreams are scary, upsetting, and can seem very real, so it's natural to feel scared by them. Do your magic. With preschoolers and young school-age kids who have vivid imaginations, the magical powers of your love and protection can work wonders. You might be able to make the pretend monsters disappear with a dose of pretend monster spray. ... A bedside flashlight can be a good nightmare-chaser. ... offer a favorite stuffed animal to hold, a blanket, pillow, nightlight, or dreamcatcher, or play soft music. ... Talking about it — maybe even drawing the dream or writing about it — in the daylight can help scary images lose their power. Your child might enjoy thinking up a new (more satisfying) ending to the scary dream. ... This might include a bath, a snuggle from you, reading, or some quiet talk about the pleasant events of the day.
sources.supports: Preschoolers begin to understand a nightmare is only a dream but knowing that does not prevent fear, because the images are fresh and seem real; label it and comfort; it is natural to feel scared; with vivid imaginations, pretend magic such as a pretend spray can help; a bedside flashlight as a nightmare-chaser; a dreamcatcher can help; drawing the dream and a new ending in daylight; reading in the bedtime routine.

sources.quote: Nightmares aren't completely preventable, but parents can set the stage for a peaceful night's rest. ... Some may happen when a child has stress or is dealing with a change. Events or situations that might feel unsettling — such as moving, attending a new school, the birth of a sibling , or family tensions — might also be reflected in unsettling dreams. ... For some kids, especially those with a good imagination, reading scary books or watching scary movies or TV shows just before bedtime can lead to nightmares. ... Parents can't prevent nightmares, but can help kids get a good night's sleep — and that encourages sweet dreams. To help them relax when it's time to sleep, be sure that kids: have a regular bedtime and wake-up time have a sleep routine that helps them slow down and feel safe and secure as they drift off to sleep. This might include a bath, a snuggle from you, reading, or some quiet talk about the pleasant events of the day. ... avoid scary movies, TV shows, and stories before bed — especially if they've triggered nightmares before avoid screentime such as video games or social media avoid caffeine (found in coffee, tea, chocolate, and sodas), which can disturb sleep

claims.wording_he: את החלום לא בוחרים את הערב שלפניו כן
claims.supports: Our recap of KidsHealth's point that parents cannot prevent nightmares but can help kids get a good night's sleep; no promise of a result.

claims.wording_he: אפשר לעזור לה גם בסיפור אישי
claims.supports: KidsHealth lists reading in a sleep routine that helps children slow down and feel safe as they drift off. That the story is personalised, with the child as the hero, is our wording.

claims.wording_he: ספר שבו הילדה שלך היא הגיבורה
claims.supports: The child's name is in the text and the child stars in every illustration (live site FAQ, 24 Oct 2026). No brand or title on the slide.

versions.conversion_rationale: הכריכה פונה ישר לאמא שנמצאת במצב הזה ומבטיחה 6 דברים כבר הערב. זה המסלול היחיד בחבילה שמדבר על הערב שלפני ולא על הלילה, והסיכום ״את החלום לא בוחרים את הערב שלפניו כן״ הוא שורה ששומרים. מאיה מחייכת לעדשה עם הארנב.
